title: Cash Book
description: Class 11 Accountancy: meaning and types of cash book — single, double and triple column — contra entries, the petty cash book and the imprest system, with worked examples.

topics.title: Meaning and Single & Double Column Cash Books
topics.concept:
A business has so many cash transactions that recording each one in the journal would be clumsy. So cash is given its own special book — the cash book. The cash book is unique: it is both a journal and a ledger. It is a journal because cash transactions are first recorded in it, and a ledger because it also serves as the cash account (no separate cash account is opened).

Like any account it has two sides: the debit side records receipts (cash coming in) and the credit side records payments (cash going out). Because you cannot pay out more cash than you have, the cash book always shows a debit balance or nil — never a credit balance.

There are several types by the number of amount columns:

  • Single column cash book — one amount column on each side, recording only cash transactions. It is exactly like a cash account.
  • Double column cash book — two amount columns on each side. The common form has a cash column and a bank column, recording both cash and bank transactions together. (Another form pairs cash with a discount column.)

The double (cash + bank) column book is very practical because most firms keep money both in hand and at the bank. A cheque received and a cheque paid both run through the bank column; notes and coins run through the cash column.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why is the cash book said to be both a journal and a ledger?
examples.solution:
It does two jobs.

  • Journal: cash transactions are first recorded here.
  • Ledger: it also acts as the cash account (no separate one is kept).
examples.answer: Because cash transactions are first recorded in it (journal) and it also serves as the cash account (ledger).

examples.problem: Example 2: Can the cash book ever show a credit balance? Why?
examples.solution:
Cash cannot go negative.

  • You cannot pay out more cash than you have.
  • So the cash book shows a debit balance or nil, never a credit balance.
examples.answer: No — you cannot pay out more cash than you hold, so it shows a debit balance or nil.

examples.problem: Example 3: On which side is a cash receipt recorded?
examples.solution:
Receipts = debit.

  • Cash coming in is recorded on the debit side.

recap:
• Cash book = both a journal and a ledger; the cash account itself (no separate cash account).
  • Debit side = receipts; credit side = payments. Always a debit balance or nil (never credit).
  • Single column = cash only; double column = cash + bank (or cash + discount).

quiz.q: The cash book records receipts on the ____ side.
quiz.explanation: Receipts go on the debit side; payments on the credit side.

quiz.q: A double column cash book usually has columns for cash and:
quiz.explanation: The common double column book has cash and bank columns.

topics.title: Triple Column Cash Book and Contra Entries
topics.concept:
The triple column cash book has three amount columns on each side: discount, cash and bank. It is the most complete cash book, recording cash transactions, bank transactions and the cash discount allowed/received, all together.

  • The discount column on the debit side records discount allowed (an expense, given to debtors who pay us).
  • The discount column on the credit side records discount received (a gain, from creditors we pay).
  • Important: the discount columns are not balanced — they are only totalled. The debit total is posted to Discount Allowed A/c and the credit total to Discount Received A/c.

A key idea here is the contra entry. When money moves between cash and bank of the same business — cash deposited into the bank, or cash withdrawn from the bank for office use — both the debit and the credit are inside the cash book itself. Such an entry is marked with the letter "C" in the L.F. column and is called a contra entry.

  • Cash deposited into bank: Bank column (Dr side) and Cash column (Cr side) — written as "To Cash" on the debit side and "By Bank" on the credit side.
  • Cash withdrawn from bank for office use: the reverse — Cash column (Dr) and Bank column (Cr).

Because both effects are already inside the cash book, a contra entry needs no further posting to the ledger — that is what the "C" signals.

examples.problem: Example 1: Which three columns does a triple column cash book have on each side?
Example 2: Rs 10,000 cash is deposited into the bank. What kind of entry is this and how is it marked?
examples.solution:
Money moves within the business.

  • Cash and bank are both inside the cash book → a contra entry.
  • It is marked 'C' in the L.F. column.
examples.answer: A contra entry (Bank Dr, Cash Cr), marked 'C' in the L.F. column.

examples.problem: Example 3: Are the discount columns of a triple column cash book balanced?
examples.solution:
Only totalled.

  • The discount columns are totalled, not balanced.
  • Totals go to Discount Allowed and Discount Received accounts.
examples.answer: No — they are only totalled (and posted to the discount accounts), not balanced.

recap:
• Triple column cash book: discount + cash + bank columns each side. Discount allowed (Dr), discount received (Cr); discount columns are totalled, not balanced.
  • Contra entry: money moved between cash & bank of the same firm; marked "C"; needs no further ledger posting.

quiz.q: Discount allowed is recorded in the discount column on the ____ side.
quiz.explanation: Discount allowed (an expense) appears on the debit side.

quiz.q: A contra entry is marked with the letter:
quiz.explanation: Contra entries are marked 'C' in the L.F. column.

topics.title: Petty Cash Book and the Imprest System
topics.concept:
Every office has many small payments — postage, stationery, conveyance, tea, cartage. Passing each through the main cash book would clutter it. So a separate petty cash book is kept by a petty cashier to record these small day-to-day expenses.

The petty cash book usually has an analytical (columnar) format: one column receives the money, and several analysis columns classify the payments (postage, printing & stationery, conveyance, sundries, etc.). At period-end each column is totalled and posted to the relevant expense account — saving the main ledger from dozens of tiny entries.

The petty cashier is funded through the imprest system:

  • The main cashier gives the petty cashier a fixed sum (the imprest amount) for a period, say Rs 2,000 for a month.
  • The petty cashier spends it on small items and keeps the vouchers.
  • At the end of the period, the main cashier reimburses exactly what was spent, restoring the balance back to the original imprest amount.

So if Rs 1,700 was spent out of Rs 2,000, the petty cashier is given Rs 1,700 to start the next period again with Rs 2,000. The beauty of the imprest system is control: the petty cashier never holds more than the fixed amount, every payment is vouched, and the reimbursement equals the total expenses — making fraud and overspending easy to spot.

examples.problem: Example 1: What kind of expenses are recorded in the petty cash book?
examples.solution:
Small, frequent ones.

  • Small day-to-day payments: postage, stationery, conveyance, cartage, tea.
examples.answer: Small, frequent day-to-day expenses such as postage, stationery and conveyance.

examples.problem: Example 2: Under the imprest system, the imprest is Rs 2,000 and Rs 1,650 is spent in the month. How much is reimbursed?
examples.solution:
Restore to the imprest.

  • Reimbursement = amount spent = Rs 1,650.
  • This brings the balance back to Rs 2,000.
examples.answer: Rs 1,650 (equal to the amount spent), restoring the imprest to Rs 2,000.

examples.problem: Example 3: State one advantage of the imprest system.
examples.solution:
It is about control.

  • The petty cashier never holds more than the fixed amount, and every payment is vouched.
examples.answer: It gives strong control — the petty cashier holds only a fixed sum and all payments are vouched and checked.

recap:
• Petty cash book: records small, frequent expenses; usually analytical (analysis columns posted to expense accounts).
  • Imprest system: petty cashier starts with a fixed imprest amount; at period-end is reimbursed exactly what was spent, restoring the imprest.
  • Benefit = control: fixed float, every payment vouched.

quiz.explanation: It records small, frequent expenses like postage and stationery.

quiz.q: Under the imprest system, the reimbursement equals:
quiz.explanation: The petty cashier is reimbursed exactly what was spent, restoring the imprest.

questions.q: The cash book is:
options: Both a journal and a ledger
questions.explanation: It is both a journal and a ledger (the cash account itself).

questions.q: Receipts are recorded on the ____ side of the cash book.
questions.explanation: Receipts → debit side; payments → credit side.

questions.q: The cash book can never show a:
questions.explanation: You cannot pay out more cash than you hold.

questions.q: A single column cash book records only:
questions.explanation: It has one column for cash only.

questions.q: A double column cash book commonly has columns for cash and:
questions.explanation: Cash and bank columns.

questions.q: A triple column cash book has columns for:
questions.explanation: Discount, cash and bank columns.

questions.q: Discount allowed appears in the discount column on the ____ side.
questions.explanation: Discount allowed (an expense) is on the debit side.

questions.q: Discount received appears on the ____ side.
questions.explanation: Discount received (a gain) is on the credit side.

questions.q: The discount columns of a cash book are:
questions.explanation: They are totalled and posted, not balanced.

questions.q: Cash deposited into the bank is an example of a:
questions.explanation: Money between cash and bank of the same firm is a contra entry.

questions.q: A contra entry is marked with the letter:
questions.explanation: Contra entries are marked 'C'.

questions.q: A contra entry needs ____ posting to the ledger.
questions.explanation: Both sides are inside the cash book, so no further posting.

questions.q: Small day-to-day expenses are recorded in the:
questions.explanation: The petty cash book records small expenses.

questions.q: Under the imprest system, the petty cashier is reimbursed:
options: A fixed amount regardless of spending
questions.explanation: Reimbursement equals the amount spent, restoring the imprest.

questions.q: The petty cash book usually uses an ____ format.
questions.explanation: Analysis columns classify the small expenses.

questions.q: A firm receives a cheque from a customer and deposits it the same day. In a triple column cash book it is recorded in the:
questions.explanation: A cheque banked at once is a receipt through the bank — bank column, debit side.

questions.q: Received Rs 4,900 from Anil in full settlement of Rs 5,000 by cheque. The cash book records:
questions.explanation: The cheque (4,900) goes to the bank debit column; the Rs 100 saved by Anil is discount allowed in the debit discount column.

questions.q: Why does a contra entry require NO posting to the ledger?
options: Both the debit and credit are already inside the cash book
questions.explanation: Cash and bank are both columns of the cash book, so the double entry is complete within it.

questions.q: Cash withdrawn from the bank for OFFICE use is a contra entry, but cash withdrawn for the OWNER'S personal use is:
questions.explanation: Personal withdrawal is drawings (Bank credited, Drawings debited in the ledger), not a movement within the firm's own cash/bank.

questions.q: At month-end the discount-allowed column totals Rs 600. This Rs 600 is:
options: Posted to the debit of Discount Allowed A/c
Posted to the credit of Discount Received A/c
questions.explanation: The debit discount column total is posted to the debit of the Discount Allowed Account (an expense).

questions.q: The imprest amount is Rs 3,000. During the month the petty cashier spends Rs 2,450. The closing petty cash balance before reimbursement is:
questions.explanation: 3,000 − 2,450 = Rs 550 remains; the cashier will then be reimbursed Rs 2,450 to restore Rs 3,000.

questions.q: The chief advantage of the imprest system is that it:
options: Controls petty spending and keeps the float fixed and vouched
Lets the cashier hold unlimited cash
questions.explanation: The fixed, regularly-reimbursed float with vouchers gives tight control over small payments.

questions.q: A cheque received earlier is dishonoured by the bank. In the cash book this is recorded by:
options: Entering it on the credit (payment) side of the bank column
questions.explanation: A dishonoured cheque reverses the earlier bank receipt, so it is shown on the credit side of the bank column.

questions.q: Why is a separate cash account NOT opened in the ledger when a cash book is kept?
options: The cash book itself serves as the cash account
questions.explanation: Being both journal and ledger, the cash book is the cash account, so a duplicate would be pointless.

questions.q: In the analytical petty cash book, the analysis columns are totalled and:
options: Each total posted to its respective expense account
questions.explanation: Each analysis column's total is posted to the relevant expense account, saving many small ledger entries.
